# Evaluating the Robustness of Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models

[View PDF](/pdf/2411.14215) [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.14215v1)

> Abstract:LLMs have performed well on several reasoning benchmarks, including ones that test analogical reasoning abilities. However, there is debate on the extent to which they are performing general abstract reasoning versus employing non-robust processes, e.g., that overly rely on similarity to pre-training data. Here we investigate the robustness of analogy-making abilities previously claimed for LLMs on three of four domains studied by Webb, Holyoak, and Lu (2023): letter-string analogies, digit matrices, and story analogies. For each domain we test humans and GPT models on robustness to variants of the original analogy problems that test the same abstract reasoning abilities but are likely dissimilar from tasks in the pre-training data. The performance of a system that uses robust abstract reasoning should not decline substantially on these variants.  
> On simple letter-string analogies, we find that while the performance of humans remains high for two types of variants we tested, the GPT models' performance declines sharply. This pattern is less pronounced as the complexity of these problems is increased, as both humans and GPT models perform poorly on both the original and variant problems requiring more complex analogies. On digit-matrix problems, we find a similar pattern but only on one out of the two types of variants we tested. On story-based analogy problems, we find that, unlike humans, the performance of GPT models are susceptible to answer-order effects, and that GPT models also may be more sensitive than humans to paraphrasing.  
> This work provides evidence that LLMs often lack the robustness of zero-shot human analogy-making, exhibiting brittleness on most of the variations we tested. More generally, this work points to the importance of carefully evaluating AI systems not only for accuracy but also robustness when testing their cognitive capabilities.

Darren Rovell's tweet claims that at its peak ("at its height"), 9.5% of the US population watched Knicks-Spurs, while 26.1% watched Bulls-Jazz in 1998 at its height. The 9.5% figure for Knicks-Spurs checks out as the peak simultaneous audience: ESPN/NBA.com confirmed Game 5 of the 2026 Finals "peaked at 33 million viewers at 11:15 p.m. ET" (https://www.nba.com/news/nba-finals-2026-viewership-most-watched-28-years), and 33 million divided by the current US population of roughly 345-347 million is about 9.5%.

However, the 26.1% figure for Bulls-Jazz 1998 does NOT represent a comparable 'peak simultaneous audience' statistic. According to Wikipedia's summary of the 1998 NBA playoffs, Game 6 of the 1998 Finals (Jordan's title-clinching shot) was "the highest rated and most watched game in NBA History, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers in the U.S." (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_playoffs). The 72-million figure is a CUMULATIVE/reach statistic — the total number of unique people who tuned in for at least some portion of the broadcast — not the number watching at any single simultaneous 'peak' moment. Dividing 72 million by the 1998 US population (~275.9 million) yields almost exactly 26.1%, strongly suggesting this cumulative reach number is the source of Rovell's '26.1 percent' figure.

This means Rovell is comparing two different metrics: a true instantaneous peak audience for Knicks-Spurs (33M at one minute) against a cumulative total-reach figure for Bulls-Jazz (72M over the whole broadcast), not an actual peak-minute audience. Other sources (e.g., https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings) confirm Game 6 of the 1998 Finals had an average 22.3 household rating/38 share and 35.89 million average viewers — meaning its true instantaneous peak audience, while likely higher than the 35.89M average (perhaps in the 40-50M range based on how other Finals games' peaks exceed their averages, e.g., 2016 Game 7 averaged 30.8M and peaked at 44.5M per https://www.si.com/tech-media/2016/06/20/nba-finals-game-7-tv-ratings-viewers-cavaliers-warriors), was almost certainly well below 72 million and thus below 26.1% of the population. A true apples-to-apples comparison of average series viewership (29.04M for Bulls-Jazz vs 20.6M for Knicks-Spurs, per https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2026/jun/16/knicks-nba-title-clinching-victory-spurs-averages-245-million-viewers/) or peak-game viewership would not produce the 26.1% vs 9.5% framing Rovell used.

This is a statistical/methodological error that meaningfully overstates the gap implied by 'at its height' framing, since it compares a cumulative total-reach number (1998) to a true peak-minute number (2026).

The **1998 NBA playoffs** was the postseason tournament of the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association")'s [1997–98 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_NBA_season "1997–98 NBA season"). The tournament concluded with the two-time defending NBA champion and [Eastern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Conference_\(NBA\) "Eastern Conference (NBA)") champion [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bulls "Chicago Bulls") defeating the [Western Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Conference_\(NBA\) "Western Conference (NBA)") champion [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah_Jazz "Utah Jazz") 4 games to 2 in the [NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_Finals "1998 NBA Finals"). The Bulls achieved a second three peat, a goal unrivaled since the [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") in [1966](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_NBA_playoffs "1966 NBA playoffs"). Michael Jordan was named [NBA Finals MVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_Most_Valuable_Player_Award "NBA Finals Most Valuable Player Award") for the sixth and final time.

The [New Jersey Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Nets "Brooklyn Nets") made the playoffs for the first time since [1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993–94_New_Jersey_Nets_season "1993–94 New Jersey Nets season"), but did not appear again until [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_NBA_playoffs "2002 NBA playoffs"). Their presence was a mere asterisk compared to what they accomplished in [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001–02_New_Jersey_Nets_season "2001–02 New Jersey Nets season"), getting swept by the eventual champion Bulls.

The Minnesota Timberwolves won their first playoff game in franchise history by winning Game 2 of their series against the Seattle SuperSonics. However, the SuperSonics prevailed in five games despite the Timberwolves taking a 2–1 series lead.

The [Cleveland Cavaliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Cavaliers "Cleveland Cavaliers") lost to Indiana in the first round 3–1 and did not appear again until [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005–06_Cleveland_Cavaliers_season "2005–06 Cleveland Cavaliers season"). It would also be the final playoff appearance for the Cavaliers without [LeBron James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeBron_James "LeBron James") on the roster.

The Heat–Knicks series was extremely notable for two reasons

*   Game 4: A fight broke out between [Larry Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Johnson_\(basketball,_born_1969\) "Larry Johnson (basketball, born 1969)") and [Alonzo Mourning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonzo_Mourning "Alonzo Mourning") at the end of the game (in which the Knicks won 90–85). A lasting image of the fight was Knicks coach [Jeff Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Van_Gundy "Jeff Van Gundy") clinging to Mourning's leg. Both players were suspended for two games. Johnson and Mourning had bad blood dating back to their stint as [Charlotte Hornets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Hornets "Charlotte Hornets") teammates.
*   Game 5: The New York Knicks became the fourth seventh seed to knock off a second seeded team in the first round of the playoffs. This would not occur again until [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_NBA_playoffs "2010 NBA playoffs").

Game 5 of the Jazz–Rockets series would be the final game of [Clyde Drexler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clyde_Drexler "Clyde Drexler")'s career.

The [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "1997–98 Los Angeles Lakers season") advanced to the Western Conference Finals for the first time since [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990–91_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "1990–91 Los Angeles Lakers season"). They were ultimately swept by the Jazz.

The [Indiana Pacers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Indiana_Pacers_season "1997–98 Indiana Pacers season") entered the postseason with a franchise record 58 wins. Although they would lose to the [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Chicago_Bulls_season "1997–98 Chicago Bulls season") in the Eastern Conference Finals, this team was later named by Pacers.com as the greatest in franchise history primarily due to their record, even better than the [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999–2000_Indiana_Pacers_season "1999–2000 Indiana Pacers season") team that won the Eastern Conference Title. The Eastern Conference Finals series between the Chicago Bulls and Indiana Pacers was extremely notable for several reasons:

*   Game 4: [Reggie Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Miller "Reggie Miller")'s game winning 3 pointer with 0.7 seconds, which has been marked one of the greatest postseason moments in NBA History. Michael Jordan attempted a game winning 3 pointer of his own, but it rimmed out, effectively tying the series at 2–2.
*   Game 6 of the Eastern Conference Finals: With a win, the Pacers took the Bulls to the limit by becoming 1 of only 2 teams to force a Game 7 in the Bulls' title years (the [Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991–92_New_York_Knicks_season "1991–92 New York Knicks season") achieved this in [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_NBA_playoffs "1992 NBA playoffs")).
*   Game 7: This was the first (and as of 2025, only) Game 7 to take place at the [United Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Center "United Center").[](https://www.nba.com/pacers/running-at-the-bulls-oral-history-1997-98-pacers-pt-2)
*   Game 7: This was the last Game 7 the Bulls would play until [2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_NBA_playoffs "2009 NBA playoffs").

For the first time since [1989 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_NBA_Finals "1989 NBA Finals"), there was a rematch of the same two teams: the [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Chicago_Bulls_season "1997–98 Chicago Bulls season") and the [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Utah_Jazz_season "1997–98 Utah Jazz season"). This would not happen again until [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_NBA_Finals "2014 NBA Finals").

[Game 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_6_of_the_1998_NBA_Finals "Game 6 of the 1998 NBA Finals") of the NBA Finals was extremely notable for several reasons:

*   In the waning moments of the game [Michael Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jordan "Michael Jordan") made the title winning shot over [Bryon Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryon_Russell "Bryon Russell"). This moment was marked as one of the greatest moments in NBA playoff history.
*   It was the highest rated and most watched game in NBA History, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers in the U.S.
*   It was the last Chicago Bulls postseason game until [2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_NBA_playoffs "2005 NBA playoffs") and the last involving the Michael Jordan-led Bulls.
*   Michael Jordan's final NBA playoff game.
*   [Phil Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Jackson "Phil Jackson")'s final game as coach of the Chicago Bulls (he would go on to coach the Los Angeles Lakers two seasons later).
*   As of 2026, this remains the most recent NBA Finals game for the Chicago Bulls and the Utah Jazz.

To put in perspective, 26.1 percent of the U.S. population was watching Bulls-Jazz in 1998 at its height.

## Research findings (background — not a source)
Darren Rovell's tweet claims that at its peak ("at its height"), 9.5% of the US population watched Knicks-Spurs, while 26.1% watched Bulls-Jazz in 1998 at its height. The 9.5% figure for Knicks-Spurs checks out as the peak simultaneous audience: ESPN/NBA.com confirmed Game 5 of the 2026 Finals "peaked at 33 million viewers at 11:15 p.m. ET" (https://www.nba.com/news/nba-finals-2026-viewership-most-watched-28-years), and 33 million divided by the current US population of roughly 345-347 million is about 9.5%.

However, the 26.1% figure for Bulls-Jazz 1998 does NOT represent a comparable 'peak simultaneous audience' statistic. According to Wikipedia's summary of the 1998 NBA playoffs, Game 6 of the 1998 Finals (Jordan's title-clinching shot) was "the highest rated and most watched game in NBA History, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers in the U.S." (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_playoffs). The 72-million figure is a CUMULATIVE/reach statistic — the total number of unique people who tuned in for at least some portion of the broadcast — not the number watching at any single simultaneous 'peak' moment. Dividing 72 million by the 1998 US population (~275.9 million) yields almost exactly 26.1%, strongly suggesting this cumulative reach number is the source of Rovell's '26.1 percent' figure.

This means Rovell is comparing two different metrics: a true instantaneous peak audience for Knicks-Spurs (33M at one minute) against a cumulative total-reach figure for Bulls-Jazz (72M over the whole broadcast), not an actual peak-minute audience. Other sources (e.g., https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings) confirm Game 6 of the 1998 Finals had an average 22.3 household rating/38 share and 35.89 million average viewers — meaning its true instantaneous peak audience, while likely higher than the 35.89M average (perhaps in the 40-50M range based on how other Finals games' peaks exceed their averages, e.g., 2016 Game 7 averaged 30.8M and peaked at 44.5M per https://www.si.com/tech-media/2016/06/20/nba-finals-game-7-tv-ratings-viewers-cavaliers-warriors), was almost certainly well below 72 million and thus below 26.1% of the population. A true apples-to-apples comparison of average series viewership (29.04M for Bulls-Jazz vs 20.6M for Knicks-Spurs, per https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2026/jun/16/knicks-nba-title-clinching-victory-spurs-averages-245-million-viewers/) or peak-game viewership would not produce the 26.1% vs 9.5% framing Rovell used.

This is a statistical/methodological error that meaningfully overstates the gap implied by 'at its height' framing, since it compares a cumulative total-reach number (1998) to a true peak-minute number (2026).

June 16, 1998 More than**28 years ago**

NEW YORK, JUNE 16 -- The Chicago Bulls victory that clinched the NBA championship was the highest-rated pro basketball game ever broadcast.

Sunday's sixth and final game in the series with the Utah Jazz had a 22.3 rating and 38 percent audience share, with NBC estimating today that 72 million people watched all or part of it. # 1998 NBA playoffs

The **1998 NBA playoffs** was the postseason tournament of the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association")'s [1997–98 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_NBA_season "1997–98 NBA season"). The tournament concluded with the two-time defending NBA champion and [Eastern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Conference_\(NBA\) "Eastern Conference (NBA)") champion [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bulls "Chicago Bulls") defeating the [Western Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Conference_\(NBA\) "Western Conference (NBA)") champion [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah_Jazz "Utah Jazz") 4 games to 2 in the [NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_Finals "1998 NBA Finals"). The Bulls achieved a second three peat, a goal unrivaled since the [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") in [1966](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_NBA_playoffs "1966 NBA playoffs"). Michael Jordan was named [NBA Finals MVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_Most_Valuable_Player_Award "NBA Finals Most Valuable Player Award") for the sixth and final time.

The [New Jersey Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Nets "Brooklyn Nets") made the playoffs for the first time since [1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993–94_New_Jersey_Nets_season "1993–94 New Jersey Nets season"), but did not appear again until [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_NBA_playoffs "2002 NBA playoffs"). Their presence was a mere asterisk compared to what they accomplished in [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001–02_New_Jersey_Nets_season "2001–02 New Jersey Nets season"), getting swept by the eventual champion Bulls.

The Minnesota Timberwolves won their first playoff game in franchise history by winning Game 2 of their series against the Seattle SuperSonics. However, the SuperSonics prevailed in five games despite the Timberwolves taking a 2–1 series lead.

The [Cleveland Cavaliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Cavaliers "Cleveland Cavaliers") lost to Indiana in the first round 3–1 and did not appear again until [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005–06_Cleveland_Cavaliers_season "2005–06 Cleveland Cavaliers season"). It would also be the final playoff appearance for the Cavaliers without [LeBron James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeBron_James "LeBron James") on the roster.

The Heat–Knicks series was extremely notable for two reasons

*   Game 4: A fight broke out between [Larry Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Johnson_\(basketball,_born_1969\) "Larry Johnson (basketball, born 1969)") and [Alonzo Mourning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonzo_Mourning "Alonzo Mourning") at the end of the game (in which the Knicks won 90–85). A lasting image of the fight was Knicks coach [Jeff Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Van_Gundy "Jeff Van Gundy") clinging to Mourning's leg. Both players were suspended for two games. Johnson and Mourning had bad blood dating back to their stint as [Charlotte Hornets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Hornets "Charlotte Hornets") teammates.
*   Game 5: The New York Knicks became the fourth seventh seed to knock off a second seeded team in the first round of the playoffs. This would not occur again until [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_NBA_playoffs "2010 NBA playoffs").

Game 5 of the Jazz–Rockets series would be the final game of [Clyde Drexler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clyde_Drexler "Clyde Drexler")'s career.

The [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "1997–98 Los Angeles Lakers season") advanced to the Western Conference Finals for the first time since [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990–91_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "1990–91 Los Angeles Lakers season"). They were ultimately swept by the Jazz.

The [Indiana Pacers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Indiana_Pacers_season "1997–98 Indiana Pacers season") entered the postseason with a franchise record 58 wins. Although they would lose to the [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Chicago_Bulls_season "1997–98 Chicago Bulls season") in the Eastern Conference Finals, this team was later named by Pacers.com as the greatest in franchise history primarily due to their record, even better than the [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999–2000_Indiana_Pacers_season "1999–2000 Indiana Pacers season") team that won the Eastern Conference Title. The Eastern Conference Finals series between the Chicago Bulls and Indiana Pacers was extremely notable for several reasons:

*   Game 4: [Reggie Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Miller "Reggie Miller")'s game winning 3 pointer with 0.7 seconds, which has been marked one of the greatest postseason moments in NBA History. Michael Jordan attempted a game winning 3 pointer of his own, but it rimmed out, effectively tying the series at 2–2.
*   Game 6 of the Eastern Conference Finals: With a win, the Pacers took the Bulls to the limit by becoming 1 of only 2 teams to force a Game 7 in the Bulls' title years (the [Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991–92_New_York_Knicks_season "1991–92 New York Knicks season") achieved this in [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_NBA_playoffs "1992 NBA playoffs")).
*   Game 7: This was the first (and as of 2025, only) Game 7 to take place at the [United Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Center "United Center").[](https://www.nba.com/pacers/running-at-the-bulls-oral-history-1997-98-pacers-pt-2)
*   Game 7: This was the last Game 7 the Bulls would play until [2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_NBA_playoffs "2009 NBA playoffs").

For the first time since [1989 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_NBA_Finals "1989 NBA Finals"), there was a rematch of the same two teams: the [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Chicago_Bulls_season "1997–98 Chicago Bulls season") and the [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Utah_Jazz_season "1997–98 Utah Jazz season"). This would not happen again until [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_NBA_Finals "2014 NBA Finals").

[Game 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_6_of_the_1998_NBA_Finals "Game 6 of the 1998 NBA Finals") of the NBA Finals was extremely notable for several reasons:

*   In the waning moments of the game [Michael Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jordan "Michael Jordan") made the title winning shot over [Bryon Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryon_Russell "Bryon Russell"). This moment was marked as one of the greatest moments in NBA playoff history.
*   It was the highest rated and most watched game in NBA History, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers in the U.S.
*   It was the last Chicago Bulls postseason game until [2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_NBA_playoffs "2005 NBA playoffs") and the last involving the Michael Jordan-led Bulls.
*   Michael Jordan's final NBA playoff game.
*   [Phil Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Jackson "Phil Jackson")'s final game as coach of the Chicago Bulls (he would go on to coach the Los Angeles Lakers two seasons later).
*   As of 2026, this remains the most recent NBA Finals game for the Chicago Bulls and the Utah Jazz.

#### Home court advantage

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=1998_NBA_playoffs&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Home court advantage")\]

The [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah_Jazz "Utah Jazz") and [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bulls "Chicago Bulls") tied for the best record in the NBA. However, Utah won the season series 2–0 and was awarded home court advantage throughout the playoffs.

#### Clinched a playoff berth

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=1998_NBA_playoffs&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Clinched a playoff berth")\]

The following teams clinched a playoff berth in the West:

1.  [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah_Jazz "Utah Jazz") (62–20, clinched Midwest division)
2.  [Seattle SuperSonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_SuperSonics "Seattle SuperSonics") (61–21, clinched Pacific division)
3.  [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Lakers "Los Angeles Lakers") (61–21)
4.  [Phoenix Suns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Suns "Phoenix Suns") (56–26)
5.  [San Antonio Spurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Antonio_Spurs "San Antonio Spurs") (56–26)
6.  [Portland Trail Blazers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_Trail_Blazers "Portland Trail Blazers") (46–36)
7.  [Minnesota Timberwolves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Timberwolves "Minnesota Timberwolves") (45–37)
8.  [Houston Rockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Rockets "Houston Rockets") (41–41)

#### Best record in conference

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=1998_NBA_playoffs&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Best record in conference")\]

The [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bulls "Chicago Bulls") clinched the best record in the East, and earned home court advantage throughout the Eastern Conference playoffs.

#### Clinched a playoff berth

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=1998_NBA_playoffs&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Clinched a playoff berth")\]

The following teams clinched a playoff berth in the East:

1.  [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bulls "Chicago Bulls") (62–20, clinched Central division)
2.  [Miami Heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Heat "Miami Heat") (55–27, clinched Atlantic division)
3.  [Indiana Pacers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Pacers "Indiana Pacers") (58–24)
4.  [Charlotte Hornets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Hornets "Charlotte Hornets") (51–31)
5.  [Atlanta Hawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Hawks "Atlanta Hawks") (50–32)

7.  [New York Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Knicks "New York Knicks") (43–39)

### https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings
# NBA Finals television ratings

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This is a list of [television ratings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen_ratings "Nielsen ratings") for [NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals "NBA Finals") in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), based on [Nielsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen_Media_Research "Nielsen Media Research") viewing data.[\[1\]](#cite_note-1)

The highest rated and most watched NBA Finals series was the [1998 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_Finals "1998 NBA Finals") between the [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997-98_Chicago_Bulls_season "1997-98 Chicago Bulls season") and [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Utah_Jazz_season "1997–98 Utah Jazz season"), which averaged an 18.7 rating / 33 share and 29.04 million viewers on [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_NBC "NBA on NBC"). That series also featured the highest rated and most watched NBA Finals game, as the Sunday night averaged a 22.3 rating / 38 share and 35.89 million viewers. The [1987 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_NBA_Finals "1987 NBA Finals") between the [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986–87_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "1986–87 Los Angeles Lakers season") and [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986–87_Boston_Celtics_season "1986–87 Boston Celtics season") was the highest rated and most watched NBA Finals series on [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_CBS "NBA on CBS"), averaging a 15.9 rating / 32 share and 24.12 million viewers. Game 7 of the [1988 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_NBA_Finals "1988 NBA Finals") registered the network's highest rated and most watched NBA game with a 21.2 rating / 37 share.

The [2015 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_NBA_Finals "2015 NBA Finals") between the [Golden State Warriors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014–15_Golden_State_Warriors_season "2014–15 Golden State Warriors season") and [Cleveland Cavaliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014–15_Cleveland_Cavaliers_season "2014–15 Cleveland Cavaliers season") was the highest rated NBA Finals series on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_ABC "NBA on ABC") averaging an 11.6 rating / 21 share and 19.94 million viewers. The [2026 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_NBA_Finals "2026 NBA Finals") between [New York Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025–26_New_York_Knicks_season "2025–26 New York Knicks season") and [San Antonio Spurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025–26_San_Antonio_Spurs_season "2025–26 San Antonio Spurs season") was the most watched NBA Final series on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_ABC "NBA on ABC") averaging a 9.4 rating / 31 share and 20.58 million viewers. Game 7 of the [2016 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_NBA_Finals "2016 NBA Finals") registered the network's highest rated and most watched NBA game with an average 15.8 rating / 29 share and 31.02 million viewers.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) It was the first [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") game to draw more than 30 million average viewers in 18 years, and only the seventh non-[NFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") sports telecast (excluding the [Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games")) to have done so since 1998.[\[3\]](#cite_note-Game7Rating-3)

The [2019 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_NBA_Finals "2019 NBA Finals") between the [Golden State Warriors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018–19_Golden_State_Warriors_season "2018–19 Golden State Warriors season") and the [Toronto Raptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018–19_Toronto_Raptors_season "2018–19 Toronto Raptors season") had a drop in American viewership however combined North American viewership. Analysts cited the presence of a Canadian team (Canadian viewership does not count towards U.S. Nielsen ratings, leading to only one U.S. home market being reflected in viewership), as a factor in the drop.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4)[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) At the same time, the presence of the Toronto Raptors in the NBA Finals boosted Canadian viewership to record levels.[\[6\]](#cite_note-ca_g1_ratings-6)

For the [2020 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_NBA_Finals "2020 NBA Finals"), the ratings dropped to a historic low, with one of the games drawing only 5.1 million viewers.[\[7\]](#cite_note-yahoo_20202-7) The average viewers figure over 6 games was 7.5 million, which is a 51% decline from the previous year.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) Some have claimed this was due to the players' political activism; others have claimed this was due to the finals being played out of season caused by the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), as other sports such as the [NHL playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NHL_playoffs "NHL playoffs") and the [MLB playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MLB_playoffs "MLB playoffs") also showed a significant decline in ratings.[\[7\]](#cite_note-yahoo_20202-7)[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)

At its height, 9.5 percent of the U.S. population was watching Knicks-Spurs. 

To put in perspective, 26.1 percent of the U.S. population was watching Bulls-Jazz in 1998 at its height.

## Research findings (background — not a source)
Rovell's tweet compares two different types of statistics, making the comparison misleading. For 2026 Knicks-Spurs Game 5: Nielsen data shows the game averaged 24.5 million viewers and peaked at 33 million viewers late in the telecast during the Knicks' comeback win (https://variety.com/2026/tv/ratings/knicks-nba-championship-game-ratings-1236783260/, https://pr.nba.com/2026-nba-finals-viewership). With the 2026 US population around 345 million, 33 million is about 9.5% — this is a true simultaneous/concurrent peak audience figure. For 1998 Bulls-Jazz Game 6: NBC reported the game had a 22.3 rating/38 share, with NBC 'estimating today that 72 million people watched all or part of it' (https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1998/06/17/bulls-a-winner-for-nbc/9e4ac4dd-ecb0-4aa8-b6fd-a6f6e56535a6/). This 72 million figure is explicitly a cumulative/unduplicated reach number (people who watched 'at least part' of the broadcast), not a simultaneous peak — confirmed by Wikipedia: 'It was the highest rated and most watched game in NBA History, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_playoffs). The actual average/peak-type simultaneous audience for that 1998 game was 35.89 million viewers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings), which with the 1998 US population (~275.85 million) would be about 13% — still higher than 9.5% but nowhere near 26.1%. Dividing 72 million by the 1998 population of ~275.85 million yields almost exactly 26.1%, confirming that is indeed the cumulative-reach calculation underlying Rovell's figure. Thus Rovell is comparing a simultaneous peak audience statistic (9.5% for 2026) against a cumulative/unduplicated total-reach statistic (26.1% for 1998) as if they were equivalent measures, which significantly overstates how much larger the 1998 audience was relative to 2026 in like-for-like terms. The apples-to-oranges comparison exaggerates the gap and would benefit from clarification noting these are different viewership metrics.

samples.research:
The tweet compares two different viewership metrics, making its headline comparison misleading even though the broad point (1998 vastly outdrew 2026 in relative terms) is directionally true.

**2026 figure checks out as a genuine peak-concurrent-audience stat:** ESPN/Nielsen reported that Knicks-Spurs Game 5 averaged 24.5 million viewers — and peaked at 33 million — on Saturday night. Dividing the 33 million peak concurrent viewers by the 2026 U.S. population (~342-346 million, per https://www.multpl.com/united-states-population/table/by-year) yields almost exactly 9.5%, matching the tweet's figure.

**1998 figure does NOT appear to be the equivalent peak-concurrent metric:** Game 6 of the 1998 Bulls-Jazz Finals (the 'height' of that series) is reported to have ranked as the highest rated (22.3) and most-watched (35.89M) NBA game on record, with Wikipedia additionally noting it had 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers in the U.S. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_playoffs). The 35.89 million figure is the average concurrent audience over the broadcast (analogous to the 2026 'average,' not 'peak'), and the actual 1998 U.S. population was about 275.85 million (https://www.multpl.com/united-states-population/table/by-year). Dividing the 35.89M average by that population gives only ~13%, not 26.1%. However, dividing the cumulative-reach figure of 72 million (everyone who watched any part of the broadcast) by the same 275.85 million population gives 26.1% — an exact match to the tweet's number. This strongly indicates Rovell used the 'anyone who watched at least part of the game' cumulative reach statistic for 1998, while using the 'peak-minute' concurrent statistic for 2026 — two fundamentally different measures of audience size being presented as directly comparable 'at its height' figures.

An apples-to-apples comparison (peak-minute concurrent audience as % of population, for both games) would show a smaller gap than 9.5% vs. 26.1%, since no source found reports a true peak-quarter-hour number for 1998 Game 6 beyond the 35.89M average (which was already very close to that game's peak, given how tight the 4th quarter audience accumulation typically is in Nielsen data). This means the 26.1% figure substantially overstates the relative peak-audience share for 1998 by conflating it with total/cumulative reach, which is a different and much larger metric than instantaneous peak audience.

The underlying message (NBA Finals viewership in 1998 was proportionally far larger than in 2026) is broadly accurate and well-documented (e.g., https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/2026/06/knicks-spurs-most-watched-nba-finals-1998-among-top-ten-on-record/ and https://www.randalolson.com/2026/06/17/nba-finals-viewership-2026/), but the specific 26.1% vs 9.5% comparison mixes two different viewership measurement methodologies, which could mislead readers about the precise magnitude of the gap.

The **1998 NBA playoffs** was the postseason tournament of the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association")'s [1997–98 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_NBA_season "1997–98 NBA season"). The tournament concluded with the two-time defending NBA champion and [Eastern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Conference_\(NBA\) "Eastern Conference (NBA)") champion [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bulls "Chicago Bulls") defeating the [Western Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Conference_\(NBA\) "Western Conference (NBA)") champion [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah_Jazz "Utah Jazz") 4 games to 2 in the [NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_Finals "1998 NBA Finals"). The Bulls achieved a second three peat, a goal unrivaled since the [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") in [1966](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_NBA_playoffs "1966 NBA playoffs"). Michael Jordan was named [NBA Finals MVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_Most_Valuable_Player_Award "NBA Finals Most Valuable Player Award") for the sixth and final time.

The [New Jersey Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Nets "Brooklyn Nets") made the playoffs for the first time since [1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993–94_New_Jersey_Nets_season "1993–94 New Jersey Nets season"), but did not appear again until [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_NBA_playoffs "2002 NBA playoffs"). Their presence was a mere asterisk compared to what they accomplished in [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001–02_New_Jersey_Nets_season "2001–02 New Jersey Nets season"), getting swept by the eventual champion Bulls.

The Minnesota Timberwolves won their first playoff game in franchise history by winning Game 2 of their series against the Seattle SuperSonics. However, the SuperSonics prevailed in five games despite the Timberwolves taking a 2–1 series lead.

The [Cleveland Cavaliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Cavaliers "Cleveland Cavaliers") lost to Indiana in the first round 3–1 and did not appear again until [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005–06_Cleveland_Cavaliers_season "2005–06 Cleveland Cavaliers season"). It would also be the final playoff appearance for the Cavaliers without [LeBron James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeBron_James "LeBron James") on the roster.

The Heat–Knicks series was extremely notable for two reasons

*   Game 4: A fight broke out between [Larry Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Johnson_\(basketball,_born_1969\) "Larry Johnson (basketball, born 1969)") and [Alonzo Mourning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonzo_Mourning "Alonzo Mourning") at the end of the game (in which the Knicks won 90–85). A lasting image of the fight was Knicks coach [Jeff Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Van_Gundy "Jeff Van Gundy") clinging to Mourning's leg. Both players were suspended for two games. Johnson and Mourning had bad blood dating back to their stint as [Charlotte Hornets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Hornets "Charlotte Hornets") teammates.
*   Game 5: The New York Knicks became the fourth seventh seed to knock off a second seeded team in the first round of the playoffs. This would not occur again until [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_NBA_playoffs "2010 NBA playoffs").

Game 5 of the Jazz–Rockets series would be the final game of [Clyde Drexler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clyde_Drexler "Clyde Drexler")'s career.

The [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "1997–98 Los Angeles Lakers season") advanced to the Western Conference Finals for the first time since [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990–91_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "1990–91 Los Angeles Lakers season"). They were ultimately swept by the Jazz.

The [Indiana Pacers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Indiana_Pacers_season "1997–98 Indiana Pacers season") entered the postseason with a franchise record 58 wins. Although they would lose to the [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Chicago_Bulls_season "1997–98 Chicago Bulls season") in the Eastern Conference Finals, this team was later named by Pacers.com as the greatest in franchise history primarily due to their record, even better than the [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999–2000_Indiana_Pacers_season "1999–2000 Indiana Pacers season") team that won the Eastern Conference Title. The Eastern Conference Finals series between the Chicago Bulls and Indiana Pacers was extremely notable for several reasons:

*   Game 4: [Reggie Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Miller "Reggie Miller")'s game winning 3 pointer with 0.7 seconds, which has been marked one of the greatest postseason moments in NBA History. Michael Jordan attempted a game winning 3 pointer of his own, but it rimmed out, effectively tying the series at 2–2.
*   Game 6 of the Eastern Conference Finals: With a win, the Pacers took the Bulls to the limit by becoming 1 of only 2 teams to force a Game 7 in the Bulls' title years (the [Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991–92_New_York_Knicks_season "1991–92 New York Knicks season") achieved this in [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_NBA_playoffs "1992 NBA playoffs")).
*   Game 7: This was the first (and as of 2025, only) Game 7 to take place at the [United Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Center "United Center").[](https://www.nba.com/pacers/running-at-the-bulls-oral-history-1997-98-pacers-pt-2)
*   Game 7: This was the last Game 7 the Bulls would play until [2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_NBA_playoffs "2009 NBA playoffs").

For the first time since [1989 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_NBA_Finals "1989 NBA Finals"), there was a rematch of the same two teams: the [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Chicago_Bulls_season "1997–98 Chicago Bulls season") and the [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Utah_Jazz_season "1997–98 Utah Jazz season"). This would not happen again until [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_NBA_Finals "2014 NBA Finals").

[Game 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_6_of_the_1998_NBA_Finals "Game 6 of the 1998 NBA Finals") of the NBA Finals was extremely notable for several reasons:

*   In the waning moments of the game [Michael Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jordan "Michael Jordan") made the title winning shot over [Bryon Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryon_Russell "Bryon Russell"). This moment was marked as one of the greatest moments in NBA playoff history.
*   It was the highest rated and most watched game in NBA History, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers in the U.S.
*   It was the last Chicago Bulls postseason game until [2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_NBA_playoffs "2005 NBA playoffs") and the last involving the Michael Jordan-led Bulls.
*   Michael Jordan's final NBA playoff game.
*   [Phil Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Jackson "Phil Jackson")'s final game as coach of the Chicago Bulls (he would go on to coach the Los Angeles Lakers two seasons later).
*   As of 2026, this remains the most recent NBA Finals game for the Chicago Bulls and the Utah Jazz.

## Post

At its height, 9.5 percent of the U.S. population was watching Knicks-Spurs. 

To put in perspective, 26.1 percent of the U.S. population was watching Bulls-Jazz in 1998 at its height.

## Research findings (background — not a source)
The tweet compares two different viewership metrics, making its headline comparison misleading even though the broad point (1998 vastly outdrew 2026 in relative terms) is directionally true.

**2026 figure checks out as a genuine peak-concurrent-audience stat:** ESPN/Nielsen reported that Knicks-Spurs Game 5 averaged 24.5 million viewers — and peaked at 33 million — on Saturday night. Dividing the 33 million peak concurrent viewers by the 2026 U.S. population (~342-346 million, per https://www.multpl.com/united-states-population/table/by-year) yields almost exactly 9.5%, matching the tweet's figure.

**1998 figure does NOT appear to be the equivalent peak-concurrent metric:** Game 6 of the 1998 Bulls-Jazz Finals (the 'height' of that series) is reported to have ranked as the highest rated (22.3) and most-watched (35.89M) NBA game on record, with Wikipedia additionally noting it had 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers in the U.S. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_playoffs). The 35.89 million figure is the average concurrent audience over the broadcast (analogous to the 2026 'average,' not 'peak'), and the actual 1998 U.S. population was about 275.85 million (https://www.multpl.com/united-states-population/table/by-year). Dividing the 35.89M average by that population gives only ~13%, not 26.1%. However, dividing the cumulative-reach figure of 72 million (everyone who watched any part of the broadcast) by the same 275.85 million population gives 26.1% — an exact match to the tweet's number. This strongly indicates Rovell used the 'anyone who watched at least part of the game' cumulative reach statistic for 1998, while using the 'peak-minute' concurrent statistic for 2026 — two fundamentally different measures of audience size being presented as directly comparable 'at its height' figures.

An apples-to-apples comparison (peak-minute concurrent audience as % of population, for both games) would show a smaller gap than 9.5% vs. 26.1%, since no source found reports a true peak-quarter-hour number for 1998 Game 6 beyond the 35.89M average (which was already very close to that game's peak, given how tight the 4th quarter audience accumulation typically is in Nielsen data). This means the 26.1% figure substantially overstates the relative peak-audience share for 1998 by conflating it with total/cumulative reach, which is a different and much larger metric than instantaneous peak audience.

The underlying message (NBA Finals viewership in 1998 was proportionally far larger than in 2026) is broadly accurate and well-documented (e.g., https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/2026/06/knicks-spurs-most-watched-nba-finals-1998-among-top-ten-on-record/ and https://www.randalolson.com/2026/06/17/nba-finals-viewership-2026/), but the specific 26.1% vs 9.5% comparison mixes two different viewership measurement methodologies, which could mislead readers about the precise magnitude of the gap.
